## Containers weren’t designed for agents

Agents have introduced a new problem. Containers isolate workloads. But agents aren’t workloads. Agents are actors.

Agents make their own decisions about what to run, what to access, and what to change. Developers and enterprises need solutions built specifically to isolate and govern them, so they can give those agents real autonomy without giving up control.

Docker’s next chapter is about delivering exactly that: security, isolation, and governance, so we can all trust agents to do meaningful work without feeling like we’re always one step from catastrophe.

## Run on trust

In case I haven’t made it blindingly obvious yet, the new Docker is all about trust. [...] ### Evolving an iconic brand for the agentic era

Today, Docker is officially launching its new brand, and I’m excited to tell you what it’s all about and why we think now is the time for change.

Let’s start with the big picture. We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself. AI is creating possibilities that would have sounded like science fiction not long ago.

But it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control? Or, put more simply: how do we get to a point where we can actually trust agents? [...] ## Come take a look around

We’ve got lots to show you. Poke around our new website. Find and engage with the new Docker brand on social media. And if you want to see what trust in the agentic era looks like in practice, try Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance. We’d love to hear what you think.

Wherever this new era takes us, Docker will always honor and cherish the trust you continue to place in us. Now, let’s go build what’s next.

results.title: Trust Docker for the agents you don’t
results.content:
Docker CISO Mark Lechner connected those ideas to security in his keynote, “One Boundary for the Agentic Era”. His talk connected those runtime controls to the software supply chain. An agent consumes dependencies and tools, then creates code that a team has to review and ship. Lechner showed how a Kit manifest describes the agent’s requested access, and how a proxy can use a credential without exposing the raw API key inside the sandbox.

Managing those capabilities as code gives security teams something concrete to review. They can inspect the environment an agent receives and compare its permissions with the activity recorded during a task. Across the three talks, the common goal was to make greater agent autonomy something teams can govern. [...] Docker Sandboxes puts a microVM boundary around the agent. In a subsequent demonstration, the same attempt to reach the host through the Docker socket failed inside the sandbox. Containers still do the job of packaging and running applications; the sandbox gives the agent building those applications an execution boundary of its own.

This is what we mean by trust Docker for the agents you don’t. The infrastructure enforces the boundary, even when an agent chooses an unexpected course of action. Developers can decide how much access to grant and retain responsibility for the work that ships. [...] ### The foundation for trusting agents with more work

In his opening keynote, Docker President and COO Mark Cavage explained why giving agents more freedom also requires a stronger foundation. He described four requirements for an agent factory: containment, control, choice, and capacity. Teams need to know where agents can act, see and stop their activity, choose their models and tools, and run work beyond a single laptop.

The keynote included a clear example of what can go wrong. An agent running in a container with the host Docker socket mounted found a way to read a secret on the host. It had not discovered a new vulnerability. It was using access the configuration had given it.
